extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers and academics interested in becoming peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for researchers on what peer review is, why to participate, and concrete steps to get involved as a reviewer (contacting editors, building profiles, starting with smaller venues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core evaluation dimensions (quality, validity, relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluates "the quality, validity, and relevance of research or scholarly work before it is published."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the primary purpose of peer review (what reviewers are assessing). The article emphasizes the scale of the task (volunteer reviewers absorb enormous submission volumes — example: CVPR received 11,532 submissions in 2024) to contextualize expectations and workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic responsibility — review-to-publication ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic responsibility — keep a 3:1 review-to-publication ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a normative guideline for researchers to reciprocate the community's labor: perform roughly three reviews for every paper you publish. No formal scoring instructions, but given as a community norm to encourage participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time commitment guideline for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Time commitment: 1–2 papers/month; individual reviews 'a couple of hours to several days.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives practical expectations for how much time to allocate if you become a reviewer. Useful for planning and for deciding how many reviews to accept. No detailed per-stage timing, but provides a realistic range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact editors directly to express interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Email journal editors directly expressing interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete actionable step for getting invited to review; the article includes a cold-email template (not reproduced in full in the fetched text). Advice implies tailoring outreach rather than passively waiting for invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a Web of Science profile to track verified reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a Web of Science profile to track verified reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation to use an external profile/service to record and verify reviewing activity (helps with credit and visibility). Presented as part of building a reviewer presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with smaller conferences / venues to gain experience
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't need prior publications; smaller conferences help build experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical pathway for newcomers: pursue reviewing opportunities at smaller conferences or venues to accumulate experience and credibility before targeting larger journals/conferences. Reinforces that prior publication record is not strictly required to begin reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional benefits of reviewing (stay current, networking, skill building, career advancement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Why you should review: stay current, build a professional network with editors and PIs globally, improve your own writing, and review experience strengthens immigration/career applications (e.g., EB Green Cards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are motivational justifications and indirect guidance on the non-evaluative value of reviewing; useful when deciding whether to invest time in reviewing and when explaining the career rationale for taking on reviews.
